# The Slingshot

> The Slingshot is a free, open-source simulation of founding and running an AI startup, built for teaching entrepreneurial strategy in nascent industries, technology venturing, innovation management and technology commercialisation. It runs in the browser with nothing to install; a game takes twenty-five to forty minutes. It was designed by Ammon Salter (Warwick Business School), who built it with AI models, mainly Claude, and maintains it. He set the design, dictated the content and the educator materials and tested every build; the models wrote the code to his instructions. No studio or programmer was involved. Nothing in the game itself is generated while you play: every event, character and line of text was written in advance and checked and approved by him, so players only ever meet material that has been reviewed. Ada and Schumpeter, the two companions, are different. They run on Claude, on the player's own account, and were written to keep them from drifting; Claude was chosen for its stronger safety guardrails. Even so, a language model can make mistakes and say things that are wrong or inappropriate. The game came out of the ESRC-funded research project "Profiting from Science" (ES/X003949/1), on which Stefano Baruffaldi (Politecnico di Milano) is co-investigator and Federico Bignone (Warwick Business School) is research fellow; Federico Bignone shaped the game's mechanics and systems and playtested every version, and his research on AI ventures and Innovate UK funding informed the game's treatment of the science base and grant funding. Cite it as Salter, Baruffaldi and Bignone (2026).

Players act as the first-time chief executive of an AI startup in the United Kingdom, running the venture quarter by quarter across four years (sixteen quarters) and racing rival firms to three milestones before money or time runs out. The game builds on the attention-based view of the firm (Ocasio, 1997), with attention the scarce resource allocated between competing goals each quarter. It covers team building, fundraising (dilution, term sheets, venture capital and non-dilutive grants), market selection using the Where to Play framework (Gruber and Tal, 2017), stakeholder management and university-industry interaction: engaging the science base, deciding whether to publish or protect, and building university partnerships. Its twelve sectors — from healthcare, finance and security to food, sport, wellbeing and on-device AI — are grounded in the real UK AI ecosystem, with mini-cases inspired by firms such as Isomorphic Labs, Wayve, Synthesia, Darktrace, Lendable, Sylvera, Robin AI and Multiverse.

Three modes serve different cohorts: Seed (forgiving, for first-time players and introductory undergraduate teaching), Core (the standard game, with live competitive benchmarking, suited to postgraduate and executive teaching) and Extreme (for advanced cohorts studying decision-making under severe uncertainty). Failure and replay are part of the design: most students fail their first run, runs are short enough to play again, and players play against themselves, chasing a higher valuation with a different firm set-up each time. Three mini-games (conference booth, investor pitch, demo day) sit inside the simulation. Version 2 (June 2026) added Seed mode, competitive play with zero-cost in-class tournaments (no registration, no personal data), the Market Opportunity Navigator, the Token Spend mechanic and a venture that regenerates between milestones. Version 2.1 (September 2026) added Ada, a venture builder that turns a student's own idea into a playable venture file (https://claude.ai/public/artifacts/73ce2e0d-b7ea-4bf2-8574-fedb51786141); four new sectors (food, sport, wellbeing, on-device AI) taking the total to twelve; a Schumpeter end-of-game debrief that reads the journey report (https://claude.ai/public/artifacts/15f902a5-957a-4ed0-afa3-e48f9982b32f); rebuilt investor-pitch and demo-day mini-games as illustrated scenes; keyboard and screen-reader accessibility throughout; time-stamped, tamper-evident journey reports for assessment; a doubled hiring pool with international hires under UK visa rules; an event pool past 590 decisions; and the Trajectory Wizard, a class-reporting tool in the educator pack. Since launch in January 2026 it has been played by more than 2,100 people in 63 countries (as of August 2026). It is free, with no accounts and no student data collected. A free educator pack (an Educator's Companion covering mechanics and teaching notes, a Player's Companion, a ready-to-teach slide deck, ideas for reflective assessment, venture-matched mini-cases of real UK AI startups, and two AI assistants for players and educators) is available on request from ammon.salter@wbs.ac.uk.

## Play

- [Play The Slingshot](https://slingshotsim.org/play): the game itself, in the browser, free.

## For educators

- [For Educators](https://slingshotsim.org/educators.html): who the game is for, learning objectives, modes, cohort guidance and how to request the free educator pack.
- [How to Play](https://slingshotsim.org/how-to-play.html): rules and systems overview.
- [FAQ](https://slingshotsim.org/faq.html): short answers on cost, session length, courses, assessment, accessibility, Ada and the Schumpeter debrief.
- [UK AI Ecosystem](https://slingshotsim.org/uk-ecosystem.html): the real-world grounding of the game's sectors, funders and milestones.
